parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists describe a cross-country study that relates pharmaceutical prices or contributions to GDP and interprets the relationship as countries internalizing or free-riding on R&D returns. Both concern the same pharmaceutical pricing and public-goods setting (Frech et al.).

pairs.reason: Both say the GDP relationship may reflect general willingness to pay for health or pharmaceutical spending rather than strategic R&D contribution. Both therefore doubt the R&D-internalization or exploitation interpretation. A1 frames this as omitted variables; B12 frames it as the elasticity test conflating spending elasticities.

Both challenge whether the GDP–price/contribution regression supports the public-goods/R&D interpretation. A1 cites omitted-variable confounding, while B1 argues the relationship is mechanical because the measure is built from spending that scales with GDP.
Both suggest the GDP correlation does not uniquely support the proposed theory. B9 is about the lack of testable implications that discriminate among models, not about omitted variables.

Both touch on the welfare and cost-effectiveness basis for the policy claims. A2 concerns the unexamined sensitivity of the $40,000/QALY figure, whereas B11 asks for a full dynamic-versus-static welfare calculation.
